paper.title: Salivary fluoropyrimidine detection and selective Trpm5 mRNA downregulation in taste papillae of male Wistar rats after repeated capecitabine administration.
paper.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Capecitabine is an oral fluoropyrimidine anticancer agent that is converted to 5-fluorouracil (5-FU). We aimed to determine whether repeated capecitabine administration produces detectable salivary fluoropyrimidine exposure and molecular alterations in rat taste papillae.

DESIGN: Male Wistar rats received vehicle or capecitabine by oral gavage for 14 days. Saliva, parotid glands, and circumvallate and foliate papillae were collected 24 h after the final dose (control, n = 6; capecitabine, n = 5). Salivary capecitabine and 5-FU were quantified by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry; β-defensin proteins by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and western blotting; and gene expression by reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction. SCC-25 human tongue epithelial cells were used to examine TRPM5- and interleukin-1β (IL-1β)-related responses under defined perturbation conditions.

RESULTS: Capecitabine and 5-FU were detected in saliva. Mean instrument-derived salivary concentrations were 1.07 ± 0.649 and 1.61 ± 1.70 µM, respectively; one 5-FU measurement was below the lowest calibration concentration and was retained only as an exploratory estimate. Trpm5 mRNA was selectively reduced in taste papillae, whereas representative taste receptor transcripts and proximal taste-transduction-associated components were unchanged. Parotid Defb1 and Defb2 mRNA levels decreased, whereas DEFB1 and DEFB2 protein levels in parotid glands and saliva were unchanged. SCC-25 experiments showed altered TRPM5- and IL-1β-related responses after fluoropyrimidine exposure and IL-1β stimulation.

CONCLUSIONS: Repeated capecitabine administration was associated with detectable salivary fluoropyrimidine exposure and selective Trpm5 mRNA downregulation in rat taste papillae. These are measurable oral molecular responses to repeated capecitabine administration.

paper.title: Identification of TAS2R-targeting bioactive compounds against metabolic decline: A novel ex vivo methodology based on enteroendocrine and inflammatory readouts.
paper.abstract: Obesity and ageing disrupt intestinal homeostasis. Bitter taste receptors (TAS2Rs) regulate gut hormone secretion and inflammatory responses. This study aimed to identify intestinal TAS2Rs most affected by obesity and ageing and characterise their receptor-specific responses in ex vivo intestinal explants from Wistar rats. We have integrated previously published transcriptomic and metabolic datasets to identify intestinal TAS2R subtypes differentially modulated by obesity, ageing, and the combination of obesity and ageing. Receptor selection was based on associations with inflammatory, metabolic and enteroendocrine readouts. Subtype-selective agonists were identified through ligand affinity databases and literature screening, and their functional effects were characterised ex vivo in jejunal and ileal explants from Wistar rats. Enterohormone assays revealed receptor- and dose-dependent effects on GLP-1, GIP and CCK secretion, including both stimulatory and inhibitory responses. In Dextran Sulphate Sodium (DSS)-inflamed tissue, bitter agonists exerted divergent immunomodulatory effects on TNF-α, IL-1β and IL-18. Overall, rTas2r108, rTas2r119, rTas2r140 and rTas2r143, activated by amarogentin, costunolide, resveratrol and ethylpyrazine, respectively, emerged as functionally relevant targets. This study establishes an ex vivo platform for profiling intestinal TAS2R agonists, revealing subtype-specific effects on enterohormonal and inflammatory responses. This framework supports the identification of receptor-selective agonists to modulate gut homeostasis in obesity and ageing.

paper.title: β-Catenin Knockout in the Olfactory Bulb and Hippocampus Reveals Dual Roles in Olfactory Discrimination and Working Memory.
paper.abstract: Mice rely heavily on their sense of smell to provide crucial environmental information. The intricate organization of neural circuits within the olfactory bulb (OB) and the communication across the OB-hippocampus network in mice underpin their ability to discriminate and adapt to odors and perform odor-guided behaviors. Wnt/β-catenin signaling has been shown to regulate neural stem cell proliferation and migration during embryogenesis and adult neurogenesis. However, the potential role of β-catenin in adult OB and hippocampus in olfaction, odor-guided behavior and working memory is not known. Here, we report the unexpected expression of collagen, type X, alpha 1 (Col10a1), in the postnatal mouse OB and the hippocampus starting at approximately postnatal day 14. We exploited this finding to generate OB and hippocampus conditional Ctnnb1 knockout (Ctnnb1cKO) mice. We found Ctnnb1cKO mice displayed impaired odor habituation and discrimination abilities, whereas food foraging ability was unaffected. Surprisingly, Ctnnb1cKO mice displayed modestly improved working memory in the Radial Arm Maze test. Together, these findings identify behavioral phenotypes associated with Col10a1-Cre-driven Ctnnb1 deletion and establish this mouse line as a useful tool for studying β-catenin function in adult OB-hippocampal circuits.

paper.title: Single-Nucleus Transcriptomics Identifies Stage-Associated Differences in the Olfactory Epithelium During Natural Sex Reversal in Monopterus albus.
paper.abstract: The rice field eel (Monopterus albus) undergoes natural protogynous sex reversal, but whether peripheral sensory tissues differ across sexual stages remains poorly understood. We used single-nucleus RNA sequencing to characterize the olfactory epithelium (OE) of female, intersex, and male rice field eels. After quality control, 22,959 nuclei were retained and classified into 19 cell populations, including olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs), basal/progenitor, epithelial, mesenchymal, endothelial, and immune populations. OE tissues from five individuals within each sexual stage were pooled prior to nuclei isolation, resulting in one pooled snRNA-Seq library per stage; therefore, between-stage comparisons are interpreted as exploratory and descriptive rather than as independently replicated population-level differences. The relative representation of captured nuclei differed among stages, particularly within the sensory neuronal and basal-cell compartments. Pseudotime analysis placed immature OSNs at relatively early transcriptional states associated with ciliated and microvillous OSN populations, whereas CrOSNs were not continuously connected to the principal iOSN-cOSN/mOSN trajectory. Cell-type-specific analyses identified stage-associated transcriptional differences in basal cells and multiple OSN populations. Predicted cell-cell communication profiles also differed among stages, with male OE showing a larger nominal number of inferred interactions but lower overall predicted interaction strength. Expression patterns of ompa, gng8, and ora4 supported the marker-based annotation of major OSN populations within the dataset. These findings provide an exploratory single-nucleus framework for investigating stage-associated variation in the peripheral olfactory system of M. albus.

paper.title: Downregulation of SIRT3 Activates Macrophage Proinflammatory Function and Exacerbates Olfactory Loss in a Mouse Model of Chronic Rhinosinusitis.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Inflammation of the olfactory mucosa, rather than airflow obstruction, is a major barrier to olfactory recovery in chronic rhinosinusitis with olfactory dysfunction (CRSwOD). Macrophages, a predominant immune cell population in the olfactory mucosa, play a key role in regulating local inflammation and olfactory neuroregeneration.

OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to investigate the role of Sirtuin 3 (SIRT3) in modulating macrophage function and its impact on olfactory recovery in CRSwOD.

METHODS: Single-cell RNA sequencing, bulk RNA sequencing, and untargeted metabolomics data were analyzed to characterize immune and neuronal alterations in CRSwOD, with a focus on macrophage activation states. In vivo experiments using SIRT3-deficient mice were performed to evaluate olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) integrity, while in vitro assays examined the metabolic and inflammatory profiles of SIRT3-deficient macrophages under inflammatory conditions.

RESULTS: Transcriptomic analysis revealed that olfactory dysfunction was closely associated with the altered functional status of mucosal macrophages. During the progression of chronic rhinosinusitis in mice, loss of SIRT3 exacerbated OSN loss and impaired the protective role of macrophages in maintaining neuronal homeostasis. Mechanistically, SIRT3 deficiency enhanced macrophage proinflammatory activity, increased hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α) expression, promoted glycolysis, and reduced mitochondrial membrane potential.

CONCLUSION: In a mouse model of chronic rhinosinusitis, SIRT3 modulates macrophage-mediated inflammatory metabolism within the olfactory mucosa, thereby protecting against inflammation-induced olfactory damage. These findings provide mechanistic insight into inflammation-driven olfactory dysfunction and identify SIRT3 as a potential therapeutic target for CRSwOD.

paper.title: Redox Mechanisms and NRF2 Signaling in Trigeminal Neuralgia: From Evidence to Network-Guided Prioritization of Candidate Herbal Medicines.
paper.abstract: Trigeminal neuralgia is classically explained by neurovascular compression, focal demyelination, and pathological hyperexcitability, but emerging evidence suggests that oxidative stress may form a modifiable molecular layer within this framework. Cerebrospinal fluid from patients contains elevated lipid-peroxidation products capable of activating transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1), a redox-sensitive pain-sensing ion channel, while experimental trigeminal injury studies show that manipulation of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) signaling and its downstream effector heme oxygenase-1 can reduce allodynia, oxidative injury, pyroptosis, and satellite glial-cell activation. This review organizes trigeminal redox biology around NRF2-centered antioxidant signaling, in which Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 regulates NRF2-dependent transcription through antioxidant response elements, and examines its intersection with TRPA1 and the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.7. We then evaluate plant-derived compounds and herbal medicines against this framework. The available evidence remains asymmetric: compounds tested in trigeminal models rarely include causal redox endpoints, whereas compounds with strong NRF2-linked analgesic evidence have largely been studied outside the trigeminal system. A limited multiscale network-pharmacology case study prioritizes Cistanchis Herba as a redox-relevant herbal candidate. Independent pharmacological evidence further identifies its constituent echinacoside as the primary translational compound for trigeminal evaluation, whereas hydroxytyrosol is better regarded as a secondary metabolite-exposure hypothesis. These findings define testable hypotheses rather than established treatments and support experimental evaluation of NRF2-targeted, plant-derived adjunctive strategies in trigeminal neuropathic pain.

paper.title: Post-Stroke Olfactory Dysfunction: Network Mechanisms, Clinical Consequences, and Rehabilitation.
paper.abstract: Stroke is the second leading cause of death after ischemic heart disease, accounting for 10% of all deaths worldwide. Stroke is also a major cause of long-term neurological disability, yet olfactory dysfunction remains an underrecognized consequence of cerebrovascular injury. Smell is rarely evaluated in stroke patients despite its central role in appetite, hedonia, hazard detection, memory, emotional processing, and quality of life. The olfactory system extends from the olfactory epithelium and olfactory bulb to primary olfactory cortex, limbic regions, orbitofrontal cortex, insula, thalamus, hippocampus, broader fronto-limbic networks and cerebellum. The broad anatomical organization of the olfactory system subjects it to frequent perturbation due to stroke or other lesions. Post-stroke olfactory deficits may result from direct injury to olfactory structures, disruption of higher-order olfactory networks, diaschisis, altered sniffing and sensorimotor control, or secondary degeneration. Clinically, these deficits are manifested as hyposmia, anosmia, impaired odor identification, discrimination and memory, altered odor pleasantness, reduced flavor perception, loss of appetite, or reduced odor-guided behavior. Current evidence indicates that olfactory dysfunction can persist into the chronic phase of stroke, although a single prevalence estimate cannot be established because populations, timing, testing methods, and reporting differ substantially across studies. This narrative review provides an overview of stroke-related olfactory dysfunction, emphasizing olfactory pathway anatomy, lesion-relevant mechanisms, clinical consequences, measurement limitations, rehabilitation approaches, and future research priorities. We argue that post-stroke olfactory dysfunction should be understood as a multidimensional network-based disorder rather than a simple binary loss of smell.

paper.title: Non-invasive prediction of olfactory recovery in severe CRSwNP: a cross-compartment translational nomogram based on secretory IL-17A.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Predicting olfactory recovery after surgery for severe chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) remains challenging. To overcome the reliance on invasive tissue biopsies, this study aimed to identify non-invasive liquid biopsy biomarkers reflecting the deep mucosal inflammatory microenvironment, ultimately developing a point-of-care prognostic model.

METHODS: A "tissue-to-secretion" dual-cohort validation strategy was employed. A Random Forest (RF) algorithm screened deep-tissue proteomes (Luminex) in a discovery cohort (N = 67). An independent RF model evaluated non-invasive nasal secretions (Olink) in a validation cohort (N = 62). Bidirectionally convergent targets were assessed for continuous dose-response relationships with absolute olfactory improvement [Δ(visual analog scale)VAS] score at 6 months. A clinical-molecular nomogram was developed and internally validated using 1,000 bootstrap resamples.

RESULTS: The tissue-based RF identified interleukin (IL)-17A as a core prognostic candidate. The independent secretion-based RF model also prioritized secretory IL-17A, achieving bidirectional convergence. While canonical Type 2 cytokines (IL-5, IL-13) lost predictive significance in secretions (P > 0.05), secretory IL-17A demonstrated a robust dose-response correlation (r = 0.334, P = 0.0003) and emerged as an independent protective factor for olfactory recovery ([odds ratio] OR = 1.408, 95% [confidence interval] CI: 1.03-2.03). The joint nomogram, seamlessly integrating baseline VAS and secretory IL-17A, yielded an optimism-corrected (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) AUC of 0.793 (95% CI: [0.6908-0.9079]) with adequate calibration and substantial net clinical benefit.

CONCLUSIONS: Through cross-compartment translation, we identified secretory IL-17A as a robust, non-invasive indicator of mucosal plasticity and olfactory reversibility. The derived joint nomogram provides an actionable framework for personalized pre-operative counseling and risk stratification in severe CRSwNP.

paper.title: Odorant Receptors Mediating Benzaldehyde Detection in Mythimna separata: Functional Identification and Ligand Selectivity.
paper.abstract: Benzaldehyde (BA) is a ubiquitous aromatic volatile produced by both plants and insects. In Mythimna separata, it also serves as a male-emitted pheromonal signal that mediates male-male competition by antagonizing the pheromone receptor MsepPR3 and disrupting the perception of the female sex pheromone Z11-16:Ald. Whether M. separata also possesses conventional odorant receptors (ORs) that detect BA as an environmental volatile remains unknown. Here, we investigated the peripheral molecular basis of BA detection in M. separata. Electroantennogram (EAG) recordings revealed robust, dose-dependent responses to BA in both female and male adults, demonstrating that the antennal olfactory system readily detects BA. Candidate ORs were selected based on phylogenetic relationships and functional evidence from homologous receptors in other noctuid moths and subsequently characterized using the Xenopus oocyte expression system. Two BA-responsive ORs with distinct ligand profiles were identified. MsepOR42 displayed a highly selective response to BA, whereas MsepOR29 showed broader tuning and responded to BA, benzyl alcohol and 2-phenylethanol. These results establish the peripheral molecular basis of BA detection in M. separata and reveal that this ecologically important volatile is encoded by ORs with contrasting ligand selectivity. Our findings expand the understanding of aromatic volatile coding in moths and identify candidate molecular targets for odor-based pest management.

paper.title: Advances in research on the regulation of honey bee odor and chemical communication by symbiotic microorganisms.
paper.abstract: Because honey bees are key pollinators in terrestrial ecosystems, they are highly sensitive to environmental changes, and colony survival serves as a reliable indicator of environmental conditions. Insect symbiotic microorganisms regulate host chemical communication through multiple pathways, thereby playing critical roles in pheromone synthesis, olfactory perception, and social behavior modulation. However, a systematic review of the potential regulatory mechanisms by which symbiotic microorganisms influence chemical communication in honey bees is still lacking. Here, we synthesize domestic and international research to assess the compositions of symbiotic microorganisms in honey bees, as well as the mechanisms of pheromone release, perception, and function. Furthermore, drawing on specific experimental cases, we discuss how honey bee symbionts modulate host sensitivity to chemical signals and consequently affect host social behavior through multiple routes. These pathways are involved in regulating odorant-binding protein or odorant receptor expression and nervous system function, altering cuticular hydrocarbon profiles, modulating olfactory memory, and mediating immune signaling. This review further explores the interplay between symbiotic microorganisms and the release and reception of chemical signals in honey bees, thereby providing a solid foundation for the conservation of endangered pollinating insects.

paper.title: Benchmarking TAS2R Subtype-Selectivity Prediction under Scaffold-Aware Evaluation: A Controlled Analysis of Receptor Representations.
paper.abstract: Bitter taste perception is mediated by 25 human G protein-coupled receptors (TAS2Rs) whose ligand selectivity profiles range from receptors recognizing hundreds of chemically diverse compounds to receptors with fewer than 10 known agonists. Predicting which specific TAS2R subtype a compound activates─rather than simply whether it tastes bitter─is essential for understanding subtype-specific physiology and for designing selective bitter-masking agents. Here, we build a TAS2R subtype-selectivity model, TAS2R-SelectNet, and use it as a controlled testbed to establish two things about how such models should be evaluated and how their receptors should be represented. First, we quantify scaffold-based data leakage in commonly used TAS2R evaluation setups and identify its mechanism. Random-split evaluation inflates area under the curve (AUC) by up to 0.21 for receptor subtypes of broad selectivity (TAS2R39: ΔAUC = +0.210; TAS2R14: +0.188). The inflation tracks chemical similarity directly: prediction AUC rises from about 0.64 for the most novel test compounds to a plateau near 0.95 once a near-duplicate of a training compound exists, and random splits enrich the test set with exactly such compounds. Reported accuracies obtained under random splits are therefore likely optimistic, and the effect can be diagnosed in any benchmark with a simple similarity analysis. Second, we show that the widely assumed benefit of restricting protein language model embeddings to binding-pocket residues does not hold for this task, using controls that isolate what the receptor encoder actually exploits. A single residue drawn at random from outside the pocket performs as well as the pocket itself (0.735 ± 0.010 versus 0.721 ± 0.010 for a single-pocket residue), and for TAS2R14 the cholesterol-binding site and the intracellular agonist site are interchangeable (0.738 versus 0.739). At matched input dimensionality, full-sequence ESM-2 pooling (0.759 ± 0.004) leads pocket pooling (0.741 ± 0.004), with one-hot encoding between them (0.744 ± 0.011); the same holds for receptors held out entirely from training. Sweeping the receptor-encoder input width from 32 to 5120 dimensions across seven representations shows why such comparisons are fragile: all 42 settings fall within 0.708-0.771 macro AUC and the ranking changes with width, while training AUC reaches 1.000 throughout, so at this data set size, the model memorizes the training associations irrespective of receptor encoding. Comparisons between receptor representations therefore require matched input dimensionality and are not established by a single setting. We further test the model on held-out literature agonists absent from BitterDB, where it recovers the correct receptor for data-rich subtypes and fails for the near-orphan TAS2R2, delimiting the class-imbalance regime, and we release predictions and a selectivity index for all 14,835 compound-receptor pairs. TAS2R-SelectNet and all code are freely available at https://github.com/tysonyj/TAS2R-SelectNet.

paper.title: Global practices in paediatric olfactory dysfunction: a cross-sectional survey of paediatric ENT surgeons.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Olfactory dysfunction (OD) in children remains underdiagnosed and poorly characterised. Despite its known impacts on nutrition, quality of life, safety awareness, and psychosocial development, no standardised diagnostic or management pathway currently exists for paediatric OD. This study aimed to characterise global practice patterns and identify diagnostic and therapeutic challenges unique to paediatric care.

METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL: A 44-item cross-sectional online survey was distributed to a verified international network of paediatric otolaryngologists across 36 countries via a closed professional platform. The survey assessed five domains: diagnostic practices, management protocols, technology and innovation, education and training, and barriers to effective care. Regional grouping was used to facilitate meaningful statistical comparisons. Categorical variables were evaluated using chi-square tests, with odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals reported for significant findings.

RESULTS: Of 351 potential participants, 167 responded (47.6% response rate). Most respondents (83%) reported seeing children with OD, yet 95% saw fewer than ten such patients annually. Psychophysical testing was never performed by 54.8% of respondents, while 88.4% routinely ordered cross-sectional imaging. Testing frequency increased significantly with patient age (Cochran's Q p < .001). The most common barriers to objective testing were insufficient training (44.3%), time constraints (29.9%), and funding limitations (28.1%). Multidisciplinary collaboration was negligible. Significant regional variation was observed across most practice domains.

CONCLUSIONS: Paediatric OD care is characterised by functional underinvestigation, fragmented multidisciplinary collaboration, and systemic educational gaps. These findings support urgent development of standardised clinical guidelines, age-appropriate validated assessment tools, and formal interdisciplinary care pathways.

paper.title: The relative efficacy of sensory modalities in driving insulin release, salivary secretion, appetite, and food intake: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Food sensory stimulation may influence eating behavior, but the effects of different stimulation patterns have not been systematically compared.

OBJECTIVE: To quantify the effects of food sensory stimulation on insulin release, salivary secretion, appetite, and food intake, and compare the efficacy of those sensory modalities.

METHODS: We systematically searched five databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, and Embase) for controlled human studies comparing visual, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, modified sham-feeding, or multisensory stimulation. Studies without an eligible comparator or relevant outcome were excluded. RCTs and non-RCTs were synthesized separately using random-effects meta-analysis when compatible numerical data were available and otherwise summarized qualitatively.

RESULTS: We included 22 reports comprising 24 studies (6 RCTs, 18 non-RCTs) and 1008 adults (413 men, 595 women). Participants were predominantly healthy; two cohorts were women with obesity. The oldest cohort had a mean age of 72.4 years. RCTs showed increased salivary secretion (SMD=1.04, 95% CI [0.64, 1.45], P<0.0001) but no clear overall effect on food intake (SMD=0.32, 95% CI [-0.25, 0.88], P=0.2742). Insulin release and appetite were each assessed in one RCT and synthesized narratively. Non-RCTs indicated increases in insulin release (SMD=0.95, 95% CI [0.24, 1.66], P=0.0088), salivary secretion (SMD=0.78, 95% CI [0.38, 1.18], P=0.0002), appetite (SMD=0.54, 95% CI [0.29, 0.79], P<0.0001), and food intake (SMD=0.19, 95% CI [0.02, 0.35], P=0.0282).

CONCLUSION: RCT evidence suggests that food sensory stimulation increases salivary secretion but has uncertain effect on food intake. Non-RCT evidence indicates potential benefits across all four outcomes, although evidence for insulin release and appetite is limited. Further well-designed RCTs are needed to confirm these effects and clarify differences between sensory modalities.

paper.title: Similar degenerative patterns of olfactory receptor genes in the giant panda and marine carnivores.
paper.abstract: Olfactory receptor (OR) genes constitute the largest mammalian gene family and are critical for olfactory perception and ecological adaptation. OR gene variation is associated with interspecific differences in habitat, diet, and sensory reliance, yet the relative contributions of these ecological factors to OR evolution remain unclear. Here, we systematically analyzed OR repertoires across 25 carnivoran species occupying diverse niches. Marine carnivorans exhibit convergent OR degeneration, with fewer intact genes and ancestral orthologs, higher pseudogene ratios, and relaxed purifying selection compared with terrestrial species. Notably, bamboo-specialized giant pandas display identical degenerative signatures, possessing the smallest intact OR repertoire and most lost ancestral OR groups among terrestrial carnivorans. Our models show habitat primarily shapes intact OR quantity, while dietary specialization governs pseudogenization and selective constraints. These findings reveal convergent OR functional decay under aquatic adaptation and extreme dietary specialization, illustrating complex links between lifestyle and chemosensory genome evolution in mammals.

paper.title: Eco-Environmental, Health and Socio-Economic Perspectives on Cyanobacteria and Cyanotoxins.
paper.abstract: Cyanobacteria, or blue-green algae, the first oxygenic photosynthetic organisms on Earth, play indispensable ecological roles as primary producers and drivers of biogeochemical cycles, and are also sources of human food, nutraceuticals, and biotechnological products. However, cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms (CyanoHABs), intensified by eutrophication and global climate change, threaten water quality, biodiversity, and human health due to their production of diverse secondary metabolites, i.e., taste and odor (T&O) compounds and cyanotoxins. This Special Issue, "Ecology and Toxicology of Cyanobacteria and Cyanotoxins", compiles 13 papers from 9 countries that collectively advance our understanding of these issues across multiple scales. Cyanotoxins, including microcystins, cylindrospermopsins, anatoxins, and saxitoxins, can cause various hazards to animals and humans, including systemic toxicity, hepatotoxicity, genotoxicity, carcinogenicity, reproductive/developmental toxicity, neurotoxicity, immunotoxicity, and endocrine disruption. CyanoHABs are governed by complex bottom-up and top-down regulation, and blooms and cyanotoxin production are closely linked, but not always consistent/synonymous. Environmental stressors, e.g., phosphorus limitation, cold shock, and grazing pressure, selectively favor toxigenic genotypes, or can increase the cellular cyanotoxin quota, although overall population growth is suppressed. This can be explained by the fact that cyanotoxins can help cyanobacteria to better adapt to environmental stressors. When blooms disperse, demise, or are disrupted by certain interventions, the reduced biomass may increase exposure to dissolved, extra-cellular cyanotoxins if intra-cellular toxins are released faster than they are degraded or removed. We term the uncoupling of biomass and toxicity as the "cyanobacterial biomass-toxicity paradox". We propose a "3P framework", i.e., prediction, prevention, and prioritization, for the evidence-based risk management of CyanoHABs and cyanotoxins. We also advocate for more studies using multi-omics and artificial intelligence, as well as multi-disciplinary, multi-sectoral, and multi-stakeholder collaboration under the "One Health" umbrella to translate science into actionable solutions for sustainable development.

paper.title: Microanatomy of the cerebellum and olfactory bulb of the African pygmy hedgehog (Atelerix albiventris).
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The African pygmy hedgehog (Atelerix albiventris) is a terrestrial mammal with well-developed olfactory, visual, and auditory senses. This study presents the first detailed histomorphological and histomorphometric description of the cerebellum and olfactory bulb of the African pygmy hedgehog.

RESULTS: Six adult hedgehogs (three males and three females) were examined using standard histological techniques, histomorphometric analysis was performed on representative sections using Fiji/ImageJ software. The cerebellum displayed the classical trilaminar cortical organisation comprising molecular, Purkinje cell, and granular layers overlying a fibrous white matter core. The molecular layer was the thickest cerebellar cortical layer (139.44 ± 5.84 μm), followed by the granular layer (115.67 ± 14.75 μm), while the Purkinje cell layer was the thinnest (23.84 ± 5.30 μm). Distinct cerebellar glomeruli were observed within the granular layer as pale eosinophilic regions interspersed among densely packed granule cells. The olfactory bulb consisted of seven layers: the olfactory nerve layer, glomerular layer, external plexiform layer, mitral cell layer, internal plexiform layer, granule cell layer, and subventricular zone. Histomorphometric analysis revealed that the granule cell layer was the thickest olfactory bulb layer (248.30 ± 16.37 μm), whereas the mitral cell layer (17.74 ± 4.75 μm) and internal plexiform layer (15.74 ± 3.28 μm) were comparatively thin. Mitral, tufted, periglomerular, and granule cells were readily identifiable, reflecting the hedgehog's reliance on olfaction for behaviours such as foraging and predator avoidance.

CONCLUSIONS: The cerebellum and olfactory bulb of the African pygmy hedgehog conform to the conserved structural organisation observed in other mammals. The combined histological and histomorphometric findings provide baseline quantitative and qualitative data for comparative neuroanatomical studies and suggest adaptations associated with the species' sensorimotor and olfactory specialisations.

paper.title: Assessment of salivary gland function after head and neck radiotherapy using 3DCRT and VMAT: a comparative clinical study.
paper.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Salivary gland hypofunction is a common consequence of radiotherapy in patients with head and neck malignancies. Reduced salivary secretion may result in hyposalivation and may contribute to oral dryness and other oral complications. This study compared objective measures of salivary gland function and oral mucosal moisture in patients treated with three-dimensional conformal radiotherapy (3DCRT) and volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) three months after completion of radiotherapy.

MATERIAL AND METHODS: This comparative cross-sectional study included 60 patients with confirmed oropharyngeal malignancies evaluated three months after completion of radiotherapy. Thirty patients had been treated with three-dimensional conformal radiotherapy (3DCRT), while 30 patients with oropharyngeal malignancies had been treated with volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) combined with concurrent weekly cisplatin. Unstimulated whole saliva was collected using the spitting method into SimplOFy collection tubes. Oral mucosal moisture was assessed using a modified Schirmer test. Following a 30-minute interval, stimulated whole saliva was collected using SimplOFy tubes after electrical stimulation with a SaliPen device. Stimulated parotid salivary flow was subsequently assessed using modified Lashley cups with gustatory stimulation.

RESULTS: All four evaluated parameters showed statistically significant differences between the treatment groups. Median unstimulated salivary flow was 0.07 (IQR 0.05-0.08) mL/min in the 3DCRT group and 0.14 (IQR 0.10-0.20) mL/min in the VMAT group (p < 0.001). Median stimulated whole-saliva flow was 0.25 (IQR 0.20-0.30) mL/min and 0.50 (IQR 0.40-0.60) mL/min, respectively (p < 0.001). Median stimulated parotid salivary flow was 0.10 (IQR 0.09-0.12) mL/min in the 3DCRT group compared with 0.24 (IQR 0.20-0.29) mL/min in the VMAT group (p < 0.001). Median oral mucosal moisture was 7 (IQR 5-8) mm in the 3DCRT group and 13 (IQR 11-18) mm in the VMAT group (p < 0.001).

CONCLUSION: Three months after radiotherapy, patients treated with VMAT demonstrated significantly higher unstimulated and stimulated salivary flow rates, stimulated parotid salivary flow, and oral mucosal moisture than patients treated with 3DCRT. These findings suggest better objective salivary function in the VMAT cohort; however, the cross-sectional post-treatment design and potential differences in clinical and treatment-related characteristics between the groups preclude conclusions regarding causality or definitive preservation of salivary gland function.

paper.title: Olfactory differences among cactophilic Drosophila species.
paper.abstract: Divergence of behavioral traits with adaptation to changes in the environment has been well documented in many animals and is often accompanied by divergence in sensory systems. Shifts in insect host plant preference behavior, in particular, are often associated with changes to the olfactory system, including differences in the sensitivity, specificity, or abundance of olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs). Here, we examine 12 species from the cactophilic Drosophila repleta group that represent three broad host-use categories: Opuntia specialists, columnar cactus specialists, and polymorphic species that use both host types. We recorded odor-evoked responses from all six maxillary palp OSN classes using single sensillum recordings and used electropalpograms to further evaluate species in which a pb2B-like class was not detected by single sensillum recordings (SSRs). The B-neuron classes clustered largely by OSN identity across species, retaining characteristic class-specific response profiles. The A-neuron classes were less clearly separated because of weak or overlapping response profiles. Despite these shared class-specific responses, species differed substantially in response magnitude and sensitivity to odorants. A pb2B-like class was not detected by SSR in D. mulleri, D. aldrichi, and D. straubae. Electropalpograms supported the absence or strong reduction of a phenol-responsive palpal signal in D. mulleri and D. straubae, while D. aldrichi retained a strong response. Principal component and phylogenetic principal component analyses did not reveal consistent clustering by host-use category. These results suggest that maxillary palp olfaction has evolved in a species- or lineage-specific manner rather than through a repeated host-category-specific shift in peripheral sensitivity.

paper.title: Oral Health-Related Adverse Events of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists.
paper.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: As the clinical use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) continues to grow for the management of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular and renal protection, noncirrhotic fatty liver disease, and weight management, their potential implications for oral health need to be considered.

OBJECTIVES: This study examined oral health-related adverse events (AEs) associated with GLP-1 RAs using postmarketing data from the US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS).

METHODS: FAERS reports for available GLP-1 RAs, exenatide, liraglutide, semaglutide, dulaglutide, and tirzepatide, were screened from their initial market introduction through December 2025, identifying 364,274 total AE reports, of which 31,195 (8.6%) involved oral, craniofacial, or dental manifestations.

RESULTS: Tirzepatide, despite being one of the most recently approved GLP-1 RAs, accounted for the highest overall AE volume, and semaglutide demonstrated the largest proportion of oral health-related AEs. A disproportionality analysis revealed a significant drug-specific signal for dry mouth of semaglutide, while vomiting, regurgitation, and reflux-related events produced a significant signal across all 5 drugs. Sensory disorders, including dysgeusia and taste disturbances, also demonstrated significant proportional reporting ratios (PRRs) and reporting odds ratios (RORs) for several GLP-1 RAs. Association analysis of AEs showed significant associations between vomiting and taste disturbances, as well as between dry mouth and dysgeusia, particularly with semaglutide and dulaglutide.

CONCLUSION: This analysis highlights emerging safety signals in oral health and underscores the need for heightened clinical awareness and prospective studies to characterize the incidence, timing, and mechanisms of oral AEs associated with GLP-1 RA therapy.Knowledge Transfer Statement:Understanding the oral adverse effects associated with GLP-1 receptor agonists allows clinicians and dental providers to more effectively counsel patients initiating or continuing these medications. By recognizing early symptoms such as dry mouth, dysgeusia, and reflux-related irritation, providers can implement targeted preventive strategies-including hydration guidance, salivary substitutes, dietary modifications, and closer oral health monitoring-to reduce complications and improve patient comfort, adherence, and overall treatment outcomes. This knowledge enhances interdisciplinary management of individuals using GLP-1 RAs.

paper.title: Retronasal olfactory recovery during biologic therapy for chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps: a prospective longitudinal study with parallel orthonasal assessment.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Olfactory dysfunction is a key feature of chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP). While biologics improve orthonasal olfaction, longitudinal data on retronasal function and differences between inflammatory targets remain limited. This study evaluated retronasal olfactory recovery over time during biologic therapy and compared IL-4/IL-13 versus IL-5 pathway blockade.

METHODS: In this prospective longitudinal study, adults with severe CRSwNP starting biologics were assessed at baseline and after 4, 12, and 24 weeks. Orthonasal olfaction was measured using Sniffin' Sticks (TDI), and retronasal function with a validated 20-item identification test. Clinical outcomes included nasal polyp score (NPS), peak nasal inspiratory flow, and SNOT-22. Repeated-measures ANOVA was used to evaluate longitudinal changes and time-by-treatment interactions.

RESULTS: Sixty-nine patients were included (44 dupilumab, 25 mepolizumab). At baseline, mean TDI was 15.0 and retronasal score 7.2, indicating severe impairment. All outcomes improved significantly over time. Retronasal function improved rapidly within 4 weeks (7.2 to 10.4). TDI increased progressively (15.0 to 26.0 at 24 weeks). Significant time-by-treatment interactions were observed for retronasal identification, TDI, SNOT-22, and NPS, indicating non-parallel recovery patterns with dupilumab being associated with greater improvements in retronasal function and symptoms compared with mepolizumab.

CONCLUSIONS: Biologic therapy leads to substantial recovery of both retronasal and orthonasal olfaction in CRSwNP, with distinct considetemporal dynamics. Retronasal function shows rapid improvement and may be particularly sensitive to IL-4/IL-13 blockade, supporting its potential role as an early functional marker of response to biologic therapy.

paper.title: Visual Compensation in Online Food Consumption: Linking Visual Perception, Sensory Representation, Taste Expectation, and Purchase Intention.
paper.abstract: The absence of sensory information in online food consumption hinders consumers' direct taste, olfactory, and tactile experiences prior to purchase. Consequently, visual information becomes a crucial compensatory cue for forming judgments about food sensory attributes. This study proposes an analytical framework centered on visual compensation to investigate how sensory information richness, visual realism, and visual vividness are associated with consumer purchase intention through gustatory mental imagery, texture mental simulation, and taste expectation. Utilizing survey data from 1226 online food consumers, this research employs PLS-SEM, IPMA, and fsQCA for empirical testing. The results indicate that sensory information richness is positively associated with consumers' perception of visual realism and vividness, which in turn are positively associated with gustatory mental imagery and texture mental simulation. Gustatory mental imagery and texture mental simulation are subsequently associated with taste expectation, while texture mental simulation is also directly associated with purchase intention. IPMA further reveals that taste expectation, characterized by high importance yet relatively low performance, represents a potential priority for improvement, whereas texture mental simulation demonstrates both high importance and high performance. fsQCA findings illustrate that high PI can be achieved through various combinations of visual perception and psychological processing conditions. Moreover, the configurations associated with High PI differ from those associated with Not High PI. This study develops an integrative account of how visual perception, internal sensory representations, and taste expectations are linked to purchase judgments in online food consumption. It also expands the understanding of visual compensation mechanisms in digital food consumption from both structural and configurational perspectives.

paper.title: Evidence summary for the prevention and management of dysgeusia in head and neck cancer patients.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: To retrieve, appraise, and synthesize evidence related to the prevention and management of dysgeusia in patients with head and neck cancer, and to provide evidence-based support for clinical practice among healthcare professionals.

METHODS: This evidence summary systematically retrieved the best evidence on the prevention and management of dysgeusia in patients with head and neck cancer undergoing radiotherapy and/or chemotherapy. The following databases and resources were searched from inception to February 2025: BMJ Best Practice, UpToDate, JBI Evidence Summary Database, Guidelines International Network (GIN) Library, National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN), World Health Organization (WHO), American Cancer Society, American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO), Chinese Anti-Cancer Association, Registered Nurses' Association of Ontario (RNAO), Japan Head and Neck Cancer Society, European Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism (ESPEN), American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition (ASPEN), Association for Chemoreception and Taste Research, Medlive, EBSCOhost platform, Cochrane Library, Embase, PubMed, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), VIP, SinoMed, and Wanfang Data. The types of literature retrieved included clinical decisions, guidelines, expert consensuses, systematic reviews, and randomized controlled trials. Literature screening, quality appraisal, and evidence extraction were conducted independently by two reviewers. Cross-checking was performed, and disagreements were resolved through discussion or by consulting a third reviewer. The AGREE II instrument was used to appraise guidelines, the JBI critical appraisal tools were used for systematic reviews, and the corresponding JBI checklists were used for expert consensuses and randomized controlled trials. For clinical decisions, the original literature of the relevant evidence was traced and appraised according to the corresponding study type.

RESULTS: A total of 16 studies were included, comprising 4 clinical practice guidelines, 2 expert consensus documents, 5 systematic reviews, 1 randomized controlled trial, and 4 evidence summaries. Evidence was extracted and synthesized, resulting in 20 evidence statements across six themes: early screening and assessment, prevention, dietary management, exercise management, social and psychological support, and survivorship follow-up.

CONCLUSION: This evidence summary provides an evidence-based reference for healthcare professionals in the prevention and management of dysgeusia in patients with head and neck cancer.

paper.title: The macrophage as a neuroimmune sensor and effector: neural control of inflammation across tissues and disease.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Once viewed mainly as scavengers of innate immunity, macrophages are now recognized as constitutive partners of the nervous system. In neural tissue their identity is instructed by neurons and glia, and in turn they shape neural function - pruning synapses, tuning neuronal excitability, and executing the autonomic commands that restrain inflammation.

PURPOSE: Here we advance a mechanistic model built on three principles: that neural and glial signals specify macrophage identity on a shared myeloid template; that the macrophage is a bidirectional sensor-effector node within autonomic reflex arcs, both relaying neural output and generating the cytokine signals that afferent nerves detect; and that this sensor-effector arc is modular, recurring across brain, spleen, gut, heart, and adipose tissue. We give particular attention to the afferent limb of the inflammatory reflex, which now extends beyond the vagus to nociceptors and to the carotid body, an arterial chemoreceptor that senses circulating inflammatory signals and recruits a sympathetic anti-inflammatory pathway, and to the stress-responsive circuitry through which sympathetic outflow drives myelopoiesis, neuroinflammation, and sickness behavior. We then turn to disease, in which macrophage function is altered by a diseased or aged niche in neurodegeneration, chronic pain, gut-brain disorders, and metabolic disease.

CONCLUSIONS: Whether the neuroimmune circuits described here are themselves disrupted in these conditions, rather than merely coexisting with them, is largely untested, and we outline what such evidence would require. We close by arguing that tuning these circuits, rather than broadly suppressing macrophage activity, is the more plausible therapeutic goal.

paper.title: The effects of zinc supplementation on olfactory disorders: a systematic review with meta-analysis.
paper.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: This systematic review aimed to evaluate the efficacy of zinc supplementation for treating olfactory disorders, including quantitative and qualitative symptoms, in adults.

METHODS: We conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Pubmed, Embase, and other relevant databases for Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) and observational studies evaluating zinc supplementation for olfactory dysfunction. Studies published up to April 2025 were included. Improvement in olfactory function was assessed with validated olfactory tests or subjective questionnaires. Qualitative symptoms (parosmia, phantosmia), adverse effects, patient-reported outcomes, and quality of life measured by questionnaires were evaluated.

RESULTS: A total of 6 studies, including 3 RCTs and 3 observational studies, were included in the review. Sample sizes varied between 25 and 606 participants, with follow-up durations ranging from 1 to 15 months. The meta-analysis showed no significant difference in olfactory function improvement between the zinc-treated group and the control group (OR = 1.78; 95% CI 0.63-5.03; p = 0.28). In addition, the analysis of subjective perception of improvement, also did not demonstrate a statistically significant effect (OR = 0.69; 95% CI 0.25-1.93; p = 0.48). However, an individual study reported improvement in specific subgroups, such as those with posttraumatic anosmia. Adverse events were generally mild and primarily gastrointestinal.

CONCLUSION: Current evidence does not support a clear benefit of zinc supplementation for olfactory disorders. Further high-quality RCTs are necessary to determine its potential role, particularly in targeted subgroups.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 2a.

paper.title: Measured olfactory dysfunction without past-year symptom reporting: Prevalence and nutritional correlates in U.S. adults.
paper.abstract:
PURPOSE: To characterize discordance between measured olfactory function and past-year symptom reporting and examine nutritional correlates of measured dysfunction without such reporting.

METHODS: This cross-sectional analysis used NHANES 2013-2014 data from adults aged ≥ 40 years. Measured dysfunction was defined as ≤ 5 correct responses on an eight-item odor-identification test. Survey-weighted models compared participants with dysfunction versus normal scores, both without past-year symptom reporting. The primary outcome was day-1 Healthy Eating Index-2015 (HEI-2015). A National Cancer Institute model estimated usual protein intake; six secondary comparisons underwent false-discovery-rate correction. Post-review sensitivity analyses assessed cognition, sinonasal factors, impairment severity and measured anthropometry.

RESULTS: Among 3,515 participants, 531 had measured dysfunction without symptom reporting (weighted prevalence, 10.9%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 8.8%-13.0%). Among participants with dysfunction, 80.5% reported no past-year problem, equivalent to symptom-question sensitivity of 19.5% (95% CI, 14.9%-24.1%). In 2,599 complete cases, the adjusted HEI-2015 difference was - 0.09 points (95% CI, - 2.37 to 2.20; P=.937). No original secondary comparison met the false-discovery-rate threshold (minimum q=0.096). Additional analyses did not establish a consistent nutritional deficit.

CONCLUSION: Measured olfactory dysfunction frequently occurred without past-year symptom reporting, although nonreporting does not establish unawareness. This phenotype showed no clear difference in day-1 HEI-2015; protein findings remained exploratory. Its clinical relevance warrants prospective assessment with comprehensive olfactory and nutritional measures.

paper.title: Acarophagous Beetles Associated with Oligonychus yothersi (Acari: Tetranychidae) in Avocado Orchards: Life-History Traits and Responses to Infested-Plant Volatiles and Prey-Derived Odours.
paper.abstract: The acarophagous beetles Parastethorus histrio (Chazeau) (Coccinellidae) and Oligota pygmaea (Solier) (Staphylinidae) are naturally associated with colonies of the avocado red mite, Oligonychus yothersi (McGregor) (Acari: Tetranychidae), in commercial avocado orchards. However, their demographics and responses to plant- and prey-derived cues remain poorly understood. Volatile profiles vary with herbivore density, plant condition, and environment, but early-autumn volatiles from mite-infested avocado shoots and their effects on these predators remain uncharacterised. We evaluated the development, survival, reproduction and fertility life-table parameters of both predators when feeding on O. yothersi. We also characterised volatile extracts from non-infested and mite-infested avocado shoots collected during early autumn and assessed predator responses to plant volatiles, live-prey odours and prey-derived residues in two-choice olfactometer assays. Both beetles completed their development on O. yothersi, with egg-to-adult survival rates of 86.6% in P. histrio and 90.0% in O. pygmaea. Parastethorus histrio developed more rapidly and exhibited greater female longevity, whereas O. pygmaea showed higher daily and lifetime fecundity. Both predators had higher net reproductive rates than the prey, but their lower intrinsic rates of increase and longer generation times indicated slower population growth per unit time. Volatile profiles differed between non-infested and mite-infested shoots, with limonene predominating in extracts from infested plants. Both predators allocated more time to extracts from mite-infested than non-infested shoots. Their responses to prey-derived cues differed: O. pygmaea responded positively to odours from live O. yothersi females but not to colony residues, whereas P. histrio reduced its allocation to both stimuli. These findings reveal contrasting life-history and host-location strategies in the two predators and support further evaluation of their potential as natural enemies of O. yothersi in avocado orchards. Field studies are required to determine whether these traits translate into predator establishment and effective suppression of mite populations.

paper.title: Assessment of individual odorant success rates in traumatic brain injury: key findings for clinical follow-up and olfactory rehabilitation.
paper.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of sensory morbidity, yet olfactory dysfunction is often underdiagnosed. This study aims to investigate the patterns of olfactory identification loss in TBI patients and evaluate the relationship between radiological findings and specific odorant deficits.

METHODS: A total of 106 participants (53 TBI patients and 53 healthy controls) were included. Olfactory function was assessed using the Sniffin' Sticks identification test. TBI patients were further evaluated with cranial CT and MRI to identify frontal bone fractures and intracranial pathologies (e.g. cortical contusions). Statistical analysis was performed to correlate trauma mechanisms and radiological data with olfactory scores.

RESULTS: The mean olfactory identification score was significantly lower in the TBI group compared to controls (10.6 ± 3.1 vs. 13.8 ± 1.7, p < 0.001). Olfactory impairment was present in 54.7% of TBI patients (15.1% anosmia, 39.6% hyposmia). Cortical contusions (p < 0.001) and frontal fractures (p = 0.009) were strong predictors of lower scores. Notably, trigeminal-stimulating odors such as Lemon (81.1%) and Peppermint (79.2%) were better preserved compared to purely olfactory scents like Leather (37.7%) and Anise (41.5%). A strong negative correlation was found between intracranial pathology and identification success (r = -0.720, p < 0.001).

CONCLUSION: Olfactory identification deficits in TBI follow a specific pattern, where purely olfactory pathways are more susceptible to mechanical shearing injuries than trigeminal-stimulated pathways. The high prevalence of hyposmia suggests that standardized olfactory testing should be integrated into routine post-traumatic neurological assessments to facilitate early rehabilitation and improve quality of life.

paper.title: Crop Load Links Gustatory and Feeding Responses to Foraging Specialization in Honey Bees.
paper.abstract: Honey bee foragers specializing in nectar, pollen, and water collection differ in their physiological demands and in how the collected resource is transported. Here, we investigated whether physiological and behavioral differences among forager types are associated with crop load, the amount of solution carried in the crop. Alternatively, we tested whether crop sugar concentration was more closely related to foraging specialization. We compared sucrose responsiveness, sucrose ingestion, crop load, and crop sugar concentration in nectar, pollen, and water foragers at the beginning and end of the foraging visit. At the beginning of the visit, pollen foragers carried the heaviest crop loads with the highest sugar concentrations and showed the lowest sucrose responsiveness and ingestion, whereas nectar foragers carried lighter crop loads with intermediate sugar concentrations and showed higher responsiveness and ingestion. Water foragers exhibited the lightest and most dilute crop contents and the highest sucrose responsiveness and ingestion. By the end of the visit, nectar foragers showed reduced responsiveness and ingestion as their crop loads increased, whereas pollen foragers showed the opposite pattern as their crop loads decreased. Notably, water foragers also showed reduced sucrose responsiveness and ingestion as their crop loads increased, despite a marked decrease in crop sugar concentration. In water foragers, crop load and crop sugar concentration changed in opposite directions, with behavioral responses consistently decreasing as crop load increased. Overall, these findings support a link between crop load and foraging specialization and suggest a role for crop distension in modulating sucrose responsiveness and feeding motivation in honey bees.

paper.title: Odour preferences of children and adults across four diverse cultures in Africa, Asia, Europe, and Oceania.
paper.abstract: Odour perception plays a crucial role in various processes, yet the extent to which odour preferences are universal or shaped by cultural and ecological contexts remains debated. While some studies report substantial cross-cultural agreement in odour pleasantness, others highlight considerable variability. To address this question from a novel perspective, we collected data from 394 children and adults (aged 3-81) across four distinct cultures (Hadza, Pakistani, Dani, and Scottish). Participants rated the pleasantness and familiarity of 11 odours (Fish, Garlic, Butter, Ginger, Thyme, Cinnamon, Banana, Peach, Strawberry, Jasmine, Butanol). We observed both variability and agreement in odour pleasantness ratings across cultures, but overall, there was a similar level of agreement across age groups within each culture. Furthermore, the most pleasant odours (Jasmine, Strawberry, Peach) were rated more consistently across cultures than the most unpleasant ones (Fish, Garlic, Butter). Finally, familiarity was strongly and positively associated with pleasantness. These findings suggest that while some universal consensus in odour evaluation exists, ecological and cultural influences, as well as individual differences, may all play a substantial role in shaping olfactory perception.

paper.title: Representational manifolds in olfactory cortex.
paper.abstract: Piriform cortex (PCx) and its zebrafish homolog, telencephalic area pDp, have been proposed to function as autoassociative networks that learn internal representations of relevant odor categories. Recent results indicate that odor-evoked activity is organized on neural manifolds that differ from discrete attractor states in classical models. These manifolds are disentangled by experience and maintain generalizable representations by restructuring representational space itself. Modeling suggests that representational geometry is shaped, at least partially, by recurrent connectivity in inhibition-stabilized networks. Here, subtle deviations from perfect excitation-inhibition balance warp representational manifolds without compromising stability. Representational drift on multiple timescales, along with the emergence of joint olfactory and non-olfactory representations following behavioral training, further suggest that PCx/pDp encode not only odor identity but also temporal context and multimodal associations along distinct manifold dimensions. These findings support a view in which PCx/pDp reorganize representations through changes in manifold geometry, thereby supporting distributed and continual learning.

paper.title: Genome-Wide Identification and Stage-Dependent Analysis of Odorant-Binding Protein and Chemosensory Protein Genes in the Summer Fruit Tortrix Moth, Adoxophyes orana (Lepidoptera: Tortricidae).
paper.abstract: The summer tortrix fruit moth, Adoxophyes orana, is a major fruit trees pest in Asia and Europe, which rolls leaves for food and generate silk nets to avoid prey by natural enemies. As a polyphagous species whose host plants cover more than 30 species, it relies on the olfactory system to receive odor molecules for feeding and mating. However, the gene resources of olfactory genes remain limited. paper.title: Olfactory Context Cues for Procedural Skill Transfer from Digital Twin-Based Mixed Reality Learning to Real-World Execution.
paper.abstract: Mixed Reality (MR) learning systems employ Digital Twins (DTs) to replicate real-world tasks, yet sensory discontinuity between DT-based MR environments and physical task contexts can hinder skill transfer. In a two-day study, 48 participants learned Rubik's Cube rotation notations in a DT-based MR environment and were tested on a physical cube (Day 1), then completed a transfer test approximately 24 hours later (Day 2). A 2 × 2 between-subjects design manipulated rosemary odor presence during learning and testing. Results showed that rosemary during DT-based MR learning increased spatial presence and motivation while producing equivalent short-term task completion time compared to the no-odor condition. For overnight transfer, when rosemary was present during learning, reinstating the same odor at testing yielded higher transfer performance and lower cognitive load, and reduced recall difficulty compared to the no-odor condition at retrieval. More broadly, matched olfactory conditions between learning and testing produced higher accuracy and reduced cognitive load relative to mismatched conditions. These findings provide the first evidence that olfactory contextual cues can support visuospatial-procedural skill transfer from DT-based MR environments to real-world execution, and suggest that when real-world tasks involve characteristic ambient odors, replicating them in virtual training may help preserve encoding-retrieval congruence.

paper.title: Responses of Glossina pallidipes tsetse fly to geosmin, 2-pentanol and carbon dioxide odour cues.

paper.title: Smelling the Way: Olfactory Modulation of Spatial Estimation and Path Integration in Virtual Reality.
paper.abstract: Spatial cognition enables individuals to perceive and interpret spatial relationships, estimate locations, and navigate within their surroundings. Study 2 (N=19) employed a triangle completion task, in which participants attempted to return to their starting point under varying rotation angles and olfactory conditions. Results indicate that scent-delivery feedback influenced spatial behavior in distinct ways across the two studies. In Study 1, visual-olfactory misalignment produced systematic directional biases without improving absolute localization accuracy. In Study 2, distance-modulated scent-delivery feedback reduced terminal homing error but also increased traveled distance and completion time, suggesting a more deliberate goal-confirmation strategy.

paper.title: From Passive Drift to Olfactory Detection? A Late-Stage Oceanic Juvenile Hawksbill's 9000-km Journey Across the Western Indian Ocean.
paper.abstract: The mechanisms underlying the transition of juvenile sea turtles from oceanic to neritic habitats remain poorly understood, as the oceanic stage is rarely observed directly. Here, we report a 201-day satellite track of a juvenile hawksbill turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata, curved carapace length of 38 cm) that traveled 9129 km from the Mozambique Channel to Huvadhu Atoll, Maldives. Current reanalysis data indicate that 74% of this distance resulted from passive transport by regional ocean currents. However, upon approaching within 50 km of the atoll, the turtle showed a marked, active course correction, swimming against weak currents while positioned downwind and downstream of the atoll, a low-lying landform (~1 m above sea level) that would have been invisible by eye at such a distance. This pattern raises the possibility of olfactory detection of the atoll and provides, to our knowledge, a first indication of olfactory-based island detection guiding habitat recruitment in a juvenile turtle, a mechanism previously documented only in breeding females. This track suggests a potential two-scale process of oceanic-to-neritic habitat transition: a broadly stochastic oceanic phase shaped by passive dispersal, followed by fine-scale, sensory-guided settlement once the turtle nears a suitable habitat.

paper.title: Oxytocin enables the formation of preference for volatile estrous female odor in sexually naive male rats.
paper.abstract: Oxytocin plays a key role in social and reproductive behaviors, yet its involvement in the formation of odor-guided sexual motivation remains unclear. Animals received intracerebroventricular oxytocin or vehicle, followed by exposure to estrous female-soiled bedding or clean bedding. Preference for airborne estrous female versus male odor cues was subsequently assessed using a three-compartment apparatus, and sexual motivation was evaluated by non-contact erections. Oxytocin administration paired with estrous female bedding induced a significant preference for volatile estrous female odor, whereas neither vehicle paired with estrous female bedding nor oxytocin paired with clean bedding induced such a preference. Non-contact erections were observed in response to volatile estrous female odor, but not male odor, only in animals receiving oxytocin paired with estrous female bedding, although pairwise group differences in responses to estrous female odor did not reach statistical significance after correction for multiple comparisons. Moreover, the odor discrimination index, reflecting relative preference for estrous female over male odor, remained significantly higher in oxytocin-treated than in vehicle-treated animals on Day 7, indicating that the acquired odor preference remained detectable one week after treatment. These findings indicate that oxytocin does not directly establish preference but instead enables a condition in which female-derived chemosensory cues acquire behavioral significance, allowing volatile estrous female odor to subsequently elicit approach behavior and potentially contribute to sexual motivation.

paper.title: Olfactory Context Modulates Recognition and Directed Forgetting of Emotional Faces: A Chemosensory-Cognitive Perspective.
paper.abstract: Olfaction has privileged access to limbic and memory-related brain regions, yet how ambient odor valence influences memory for emotional faces remains poorly understood. This study examined the effects of pleasant odor, unpleasant odor, and odorless condition on recognition accuracy, reaction time, and directed forgetting of emotional faces. In Experiment 1 (study-recognition, n = 31), unpleasant odor significantly impaired recognition accuracy relative to pleasant odor and odorless condition (ps < .01) and slowed reaction times (p < .01); negative faces were recognized more accurately than positive faces (p < .01). In Experiment 2 (item-method directed forgetting, n = 33), a three-way interaction (p < .05) showed that odor valence selectively modulated directed forgetting depending on face type. Under pleasant odor, positive faces showed a robust directed forgetting effect (p < .01), whereas neutral faces exhibited a marginally reversed effect (p = .052). Under unpleasant odor, neutral faces demonstrated a significant directed forgetting effect (p < .01). No directed forgetting was observed for negative faces across all odor conditions. These findings provide novel behavioral evidence that olfactory contexts do not simply enhance or impair memory globally but selectively tune intentional forgetting in a valence-specific manner, advancing our understanding of how chemosensory environments shape cognitive control over socially relevant emotional information.

paper.title: Virtual cranial endocast of Lotheridium mengi and brain evolution in early metatherians.
paper.abstract: Very little is known about the early brain evolution of Metatheria, and no brain endocast of this group has been described from prior to the Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-Pg) boundary. This has led to great uncertainty regarding the ancestral condition of the therian brain. Here, we aim to fill some of this gap by describing the first brain endocast of a Cretaceous metatherian, Lotheridium mengi from the Late Cretaceous of Henan, China. Lotheridium has an encephalization quotient comparable to the Cretaceous multituberculate Chulsanbaatar and eutherian Asioryctes and reaches the lower range of crown mammals. Together with patterns observed in other Mesozoic mammals, this suggests that increased encephalization evolved independently in several major mammalian lineages. The endocast is characterized by relatively small olfactory bulbs, well-developed petrosal lobules, and a prominent hypophyseal cast, differentiating it from earlier mammals. With the addition of a dorsally exposed midbrain, Lotheridium closely resembles the condition observed in Cretaceous eutherians. We propose that reduced olfactory bulb proportions and increased endocranial volume in Cretaceous eutherians and metatherians reflect a major shift in mammalian brain evolution, from primarily olfactory bulb expansion in the Jurassic to predominantly neocortical, brainstem, and cerebellar expansion in the Late Cretaceous. The endocranial morphology of Lotheridium further indicates that several neuroanatomical features characteristic of Paleogene and extant marsupials, including relatively enlarged olfactory bulbs and a smaller brain size compared to eutherians, are unlikely to represent the plesiomorphic condition for Metatheria. Ultimately, Lotheridium provides crucial new information regarding the ancestral condition of marsupial brains.

paper.title: Short Versus Long Maribavir Treatment Duration for Cytomegalovirus Infection in Solid Organ Transplant Recipients: A Real-World Cohort Study.
paper.abstract: Maribavir (MBV) is an oral antiviral approved for refractory or resistant CMV, with an 8-week regimen used in the pivotal clinical trial. Adverse events were generally mild (mainly dysgeusia), but four patients discontinued therapy because of this. In this real-world cohort of SOT recipients with refractory, resistant, or valganciclovir-intolerant CMV infection, selected patients receiving shorter MBV courses achieved viral clearance and recurrence rates comparable to the standard regimen.

paper.title: Tissue-Specific miRNA Responses to Tick-Borne Encephalitis Virus Strains in Mice.
paper.abstract: Background/Objectives: Tick-borne encephalitis virus (TBEV) is a vector-borne flavivirus that targets the CNS and causes severe encephalitis with long-term neurological sequelae. This suggests that the pathogenicity of individual strains in the mouse model may not always correspond to the subtype-based lethality classification in humans and is determined by strain-specific features of tropism and infection kinetics.

paper.title: Is the Proust phenomenon fact or fiction? A systematic review and meta-analysis of odor-evoked autobiographical memory.
paper.abstract: Odors are widely believed to be the most powerful trigger for autobiographical memory (AM). This meta-analysis provides the first comprehensive meta-analytic test of this claim, known as the Proust phenomenon. Higher proportions of females and more recent publication years were each associated with smaller effects for evocativeness and pleasantness, respectively. Subgroup analyses showed that the advantage of olfactory cues for emotional intensity was stronger in within-subject than between-subject designs. Moreover, their advantage in terms of pleasantness was greatest relative to label cues, followed by visual and auditory cues. Although olfactory cues showed an advantage for four characteristics of AMs, these results do not fully confirm the Proust phenomenon. Overall, these findings suggest that the olfactory advantage is selective rather than universal, and future studies should clarify the conditions under which it emerges.

paper.title: Chemical functionality of food additives in sensory design, product stability and food safety: a critical review of mechanisms, evidence and clean-label innovation.
paper.abstract: Food additives are essential to food processing, contributing to preservation, sensory quality, structural stability and product acceptability. The evidence shows that food additives act through antimicrobial, antioxidant, chelating, rheological, emulsifying and sensory mechanisms that influence food stability and consumer-perceived quality. Organic acids inhibit microorganisms through acidification and metabolic disruption, whereas antioxidants and chelating agents reduce oxidative deterioration. Hydrocolloids modify rheology, water binding, gel formation and mouthfeel, whereas emulsifiers enhance interfacial and structural stability. Glutamates and nucleotide enhancers, including inosinate and guanylate, modulate umami perception through taste-receptor interactions, linking molecular functionality with sensory response. Colourants influence visual perception and consumer expectations, although their stability is influenced by food-matrix conditions. Across these applications, additive efficacy depends on the concentration, matrix composition, processing conditions and interactions among ingredients. Natural and clean-label additives offer promising alternatives to synthetic ingredients, but their technological performance may be constrained by compositional variability, stability, standardization, cost, sensory effects and regulatory requirements. Safety evaluation remains dependent on dose, exposure, susceptible populations and regulatory thresholds. Future research should prioritize matrix-specific additive design, standardization of natural and bio-derived ingredients, mechanistic sensory studies, sustainable production, predictive safety assessment, and AI-assisted formulation to develop additives that are technologically effective, safe, sustainable and acceptable to consumers. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

paper.title: Digital biomarkers derived from wearable and portable devices in prodromal Parkinson's disease and at-risk populations: a scoping review.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prodromal Parkinson's disease (pPD) represents a pre-diagnostic stage during which subtle and heterogeneous changes may be difficult to detect through conventional clinical assessments. Digital biomarkers derived from wearable or portable devices offer opportunities for objective and longitudinal assessment. This scoping review aimed to map the current evidence on digital biomarkers in individuals with formally defined pPD or populations at increased risk of Parkinson's disease (PD), focusing on measurement approaches, analytical methods, types of evidence, and methodological gaps.

METHODS: A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and ACM Digital Library was conducted from database inception to August 31, 2026. Studies investigating digital biomarkers derived from wearable or portable devices in individuals with formally defined pPD or populations at increased risk of PD were included. Study characteristics, digital biomarker domains, measurement and analytical approaches, and types of evidence were synthesized descriptively.

RESULTS: Forty-three studies were included, primarily involving individuals with iRBD or other high-risk states associated with α-synucleinopathies, population-based or broader prodromal-risk cohorts, genetic high-risk populations, and individuals with idiopathic hyposmia/anosmia. Digital biomarkers encompassed motor, speech, sleep/activity, and multidomain features, with motor-related measures, particularly gait and mobility, being the most extensively investigated. Machine-learning approaches were applied across several domains, whereas genuinely multidomain studies remained limited. Most studies provided cross-sectional evidence of group differences or discriminative performance, whereas prospective evidence regarding future PD diagnosis or phenoconversion was less extensive. Considerable heterogeneity was observed in measurement protocols, analytical approaches, and validation strategies.

CONCLUSION: Wearable- and portable-device-derived digital biomarkers represent promising candidate tools for characterizing and monitoring individuals across the prodromal PD risk spectrum. However, evidence supporting clinical prediction of phenoconversion remains limited by methodological heterogeneity and a lack of sufficient longitudinal and external validation. Future research should prioritize standardized assessment, large, multicenter longitudinal cohorts, independent external validation, and integration with established clinical and biological markers.

The BORCS8 gene encodes a protein subunit of the BLOC-one-related complex (BORC) in lysosomes that helps them to be transported to the peripheral cytoplasm in non-neuronal cells and the distal axon in neurons. Clinical features described in these cases were cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, hypomyelination, and a thin corpus callosum. We postulate that this could be due to a homozygous amorphic (complete loss-of-function) variant in our case, compared to the homozygous hypomorphs (partial loss-of-function) or compound heterozygous amorphic-hypomorphic variants described in the previously published childhood-onset cases.
